A.title: Question 1: AI-Generated Messages
A.scenario: An email from a colleague you work with daily matches their usual tone, mentions yesterday's project meeting correctly, and asks you to open a shared file. Attackers can now use AI to copy a person's writing style. What does this mean for how you judge such an email?

email.label: Message under review
email.subject: Updated project meeting notes
email.body:
Hi,
As discussed in yesterday's meeting, I have uploaded the revised project notes. Please open the shared file and review the changes before our next discussion.
Thanks

options: Only messages with spelling mistakes need checking, because AI-written text is always perfect
Messages that sound exactly like a colleague can be trusted, because AI cannot copy personal writing styles
Only messages from outside the company need checking, because AI cannot be used on internal email
A message that sounds exactly like a colleague is not proof it is really them, so check the sender address and confirm unexpected file requests another way
A.explanation: AI can imitate a person's tone and mention real details gathered from public posts or old emails, so a familiar style is not proof of identity. Check the sender address and confirm unexpected requests through another channel. The option about internal email is wrong because a colleague's account can itself be compromised.

A.title: Question 2: What Is Phishing?
options: A cyberattack where criminals use a software flaw to get into a computer without any action from you
A cyberattack where criminals try thousands of password guesses until one works
A cyberattack where criminals pretend to be a trusted person or company to trick you into sharing information or clicking something harmful
A cyberattack where criminals flood a company's website with traffic until it stops working
A.explanation: Phishing works by tricking a person through impersonation. The denial-of-service option describes a different attack, the password-guessing option is brute force, and the software-flaw option is an exploit.

A.title: Question 3: Identify the Legitimate Payroll Email
A.scenario: The two emails below look almost identical. Your company's real domain is fujisilvertech.com. Which one is legitimate?

emails.label: Email 1
emails.subject: Your November payslip is ready
emails.body:
Hello,
Your payslip for November 2026 is now avaliable in the HR portal.
Regards,
Payroll Team

emails.label: Email 2
emails.subject: Your November payslip is ready
emails.body:
Hello,
Your payslip for November 2026 is now available in the HR portal.
Regards,
Payroll Team

options: Email 1 only
Email 2 only
Both emails are legitimate
Neither email is legitimate
A.explanation: Email 2 uses fujisilvertech.com, your company's real domain. Email 1 uses fujisilvertech.co, with the final m missing, in both the sender address and the link. The sender also uses the misspelled name payrole. Always read a domain to its last letter.

A.title: Question 4: Fake Microsoft Sign-In
A.scenario: You typed your work password into a fake page, which then sent you on to the real Microsoft 365 sign-in, where you signed in normally. Nothing seems wrong. What is the best sequence of actions?

email.label: Message under review
email.subject: Your Microsoft 365 account requires attention
email.body:
Hello,
Your account requires a quick security check. Please sign in using the link below to avoid interruption to your work services.
Microsoft 365 Support

options: Change your password from the official page, and report it only if you later notice unusual activity
Report the incident to IT security, then change your password only after they reply so their investigation is not disturbed
Report the incident to IT security, then sign out of all devices and wait for IT to say whether a password change is needed
Change your password from the official page, then report the incident to IT security so sessions and mailbox rules can be checked
A.explanation: Changing the password first cuts the attacker off, and reporting lets IT check active sessions, mailbox forwarding rules and other accounts that use the same password. The other options delay the fix or hide the incident. A normal-looking redirect is exactly how this attack covers its tracks.

A.title: Question 5: The OneDrive Shared Folder
A.scenario: A colleague in your department shares a OneDrive folder called Team Reviews 2026. The notice comes from Microsoft's real notification address, but the folder asks you to sign in again, and this colleague has never shared files with you before. What is the best next step?

email.label: Message under review
email.subject: A colleague shared Team Reviews 2026 with you
email.body:
Hello,
A colleague has shared a folder named Team Reviews 2026 with you. Open the folder to view the shared documents.
Microsoft OneDrive

options: Forward the share notice to your manager and wait for them to say whether it is safe
Message your colleague on Teams to confirm, and open the link yourself while you wait for the reply
Sign in through the page, because the notice came from Microsoft's real notification address
Open OneDrive from your own bookmark to see whether the folder appears under Shared with me, and confirm with your colleague on Teams
A.explanation: A real share shows up inside your own OneDrive, so checking there avoids the link entirely, and confirming with the colleague catches a compromised account. A real Microsoft sender proves nothing if the colleague's account was taken over. Opening the link or relying on someone else to verify it does not provide the same protection.

A.title: Question 6: Identify the Legitimate OneDrive Email
A.scenario: Microsoft sends OneDrive and Microsoft 365 emails from microsoft.com. Your work account receives the two emails below. Which one is legitimate?

emails.label: Email 1
emails.subject: Your OneDrive storage is almost full
emails.body:
Hi,
Your OneDrive storage is almost full. Free up space or add storage to keep syncing your files immediatly.
The Microsoft OneDrive team

emails.label: Email 2
emails.subject: Your OneDrive storage is almost full
emails.body:
Hi,
Your OneDrive storage is almost full. Free up space or add storage to keep syncing your files immediately.
The Microsoft OneDrive team

options: Email 1 only
Email 2 only
Both emails are legitimate
Neither email is legitimate
A.explanation: Email 1 uses rnicrosoft.com: the letters r and n side by side can look like an m. It also misspells immediately. Email 2 uses the real microsoft.com domain. When in doubt, open OneDrive yourself and check your storage there.

A.title: Question 7: Password Expiry Notice
A.scenario: An email from IT Service Desk says your password expires in 3 hours and links to a sign-in page. The sender address and the link both show your company's real domain, and IT announced last week that expiry notices were coming. What is the strongest next step?

email.label: Message under review
email.subject: Reminder: Your password expires soon
email.body:
Hello,
Your work password is due to expire in 3 hours. Please review your account status through the company sign-in portal.
IT Service Desk

options: Open the password page from your own bookmark, since a genuine expiry will show there, and report the email to IT if it does not
Check the sender address and the link in the email, and sign in through the link if both show your company's domain
Reply to the email asking the service desk to confirm, and sign in through the link once they say yes
Use the link, because the sender address, the domain and last week's announcement all match
A.explanation: Even when everything matches, the safest check is to reach the real site yourself: a genuine expiry will appear there. Sender names can be spoofed and accounts can be compromised. Replying to the email reaches the same person who sent it.

A.title: Question 8: Understanding MFA
A.scenario: Your company is rolling out MFA for all staff. What does MFA stand for, and how does it protect your account?
options: Managed File Access; it limits which folders in the company drive you can open
Multi-Function Antivirus; it scans each file you download for harmful software
Multi-Factor Authentication; it asks for a second proof of identity (such as a code or an approval on your phone) in addition to your password
Mandatory Firewall Activation; it blocks every email sent from unknown senders
A.explanation: MFA means Multi-Factor Authentication. If your password is stolen, the attacker still needs the second factor. Never approve a prompt or share a code that you did not trigger yourself.

A.title: Question 9: Identify the Legitimate Google Storage Email
A.scenario: Your Google account is running low on storage. Google's real emails come from google.com. Which of these two emails is legitimate?

emails.body:

options: Email 1 only
Email 2 only
Both emails are legitimate
Neither email is legitimate
A.explanation: Email 2 uses googlle.com, with an extra l, in both the sender address and the link, and misspells interruption. Email 1 uses Google's real domain, google.com. For any storage warning, you can also check your own Google account directly.

A.title: Question 10: Managing Director Impersonation
A.scenario: You get a WhatsApp message from an unknown number that uses the Managing Director's photo and name: I am in a client meeting and cannot take calls. Buy ₹50,000 of Amazon vouchers for a client gift and send me the codes here; Accounts will reimburse you today. It mentions a real client visit your team has been preparing for. What is the best action?

email.label: Related message
email.subject: Urgent request from Managing Director
email.body: I am in a client meeting and cannot take calls. Buy ₹50,000 of Amazon vouchers for a client gift and send me the codes here. Accounts will reimburse you today.

options: Do not buy anything; contact the Managing Director or their office on their saved number or the company directory, and report the WhatsApp message to IT security
Reply on WhatsApp asking the sender to confirm the client's name, and buy the vouchers if the answer is correct
Buy the vouchers, since the message mentions a real client visit that only someone inside the company would know about
Do not buy anything; reply on WhatsApp that you need approval from Accounts first, and see how the sender responds
A.explanation: This is impersonation of a senior leader over a messaging app. A client visit is easy to learn from a leaked message, a social media post or an earlier compromise, so it proves nothing. Any reply, even a question or a stalling answer, keeps the attacker talking and lets them adapt. Verify through a number you already trust and report it.

B.title: Question 1: Suspicious Courier SMS
B.scenario: You ordered stationery for the plant. A text arrives in the same SMS thread as the courier's earlier genuine updates: Delivery on hold, pin code mismatch. Update within 12 hours: courier-update.in/FS4471. The order number in the text is correct. What is the best next action?

email.label: Message under review
email.subject: Delivery on hold
email.body: Delivery on hold, pin code mismatch. Update within 12 hours to avoid return of your parcel.

options: Open the link on your phone, but only confirm the pin code and enter no name, phone number or payment details
Look up the order in the courier's official app or website using your tracking number, and report the text to IT security
Search for the courier's name, open the first result, and confirm the address there
Reply to the text with your correct pin code, since replying is safer than opening a link
B.explanation: Attackers can slip texts into an existing thread by faking the sender name, and a correct order number can come from an earlier leak, so neither proves the text is genuine. Look the order up yourself with your tracking number and report the text. Confirming the pin code or replying with it still gives details to the sender, and the first search result can be a paid fake advert.

B.title: Question 2: Spear Phishing
B.scenario: What is spear phishing, for example when you receive a message that names your manager and your current project?
options: A phishing attack that spreads automatically from one infected computer to others on the same network
A phishing attack that is carried out through a phone call instead of an email
A phishing attack sent to thousands of random people with the same generic message
A phishing attack aimed at one specific person or a small group, using personal details such as their name, role or projects to look believable
B.explanation: Spear phishing is targeted and personalised. The mass-message option describes general phishing, the phone-call option is vishing, and the automatically spreading attack describes a computer worm.

B.title: Question 3: Fake Zoom Plug-In
B.scenario: In a Zoom meeting with a real supplier you work with, the host posts a link in chat to download the updated meeting plug-in for screen sharing. The host's name matches your supplier contact, but they joined from a new Zoom account. What is the best response?

email.label: Meeting chat message
email.subject: Updated screen-sharing plug-in
email.body: Please download the updated meeting plug-in to enable screen sharing for this meeting. Install it before continuing.

options: Do not install it, ask the host to share the screen without it, and update only through the official Zoom app or your company's software portal
Download it but scan it with antivirus before you run it
Install it from the host's link, since the host is your known supplier contact
Install it only after the host confirms in the chat that it is safe
B.explanation: A supplier account can be compromised or imitated, and fake plug-in downloads are a common way to deliver harmful software. Update only through official sources. Confirmation in the same chat can come from the attacker, and a scan does not catch everything.

B.title: Question 4: AI-Gathered Personal Details
B.scenario: Attackers use AI tools to collect details from LinkedIn, company websites and social media. You receive an email that mentions your manager's name, your current project and a conference you recently attended. What does this tell you?

email.label: Message under review
email.subject: Follow-up on your recent conference
email.body:
Hello,
Following your recent conference and the current project discussions with your manager, please review the attached project update.
Regards,
Project Coordination

options: Accurate personal details do not prove the sender is genuine, since AI tools can gather them from public profiles, so judge the sender, the link and the request instead
The email is probably from a colleague, because attackers only guess generic details
The email is only suspicious if it also contains a link or an attachment
The email must be genuine, because outsiders cannot know these details
B.explanation: Names, projects and events are often public, and AI can gather and use them in seconds to make a message feel personal. Judge the sender address, the link and what is being asked. A request for money, data or a reply can be dangerous even without a link or attachment.

B.title: Question 5: Suspicious DocuSign Request
B.scenario: A DocuSign email sent to your work address really comes from DocuSign and the envelope opens on docusign.com, but you do not know the sender, a person at Narmada Steel Procurement, and the document is titled Vendor Payment Update. What is the best next action?

email.label: Message under review
email.subject: Please review and sign: Vendor Payment Update
email.body:
Hello,
Narmada Steel Procurement has sent you a document titled Vendor Payment Update for your review and signature.
Please review the document at your earliest convenience.
DocuSign

options: Sign it, since the email and the page both come from the genuine DocuSign service
Contact the named sender or Narmada Steel Procurement on a phone number you already have, and do not sign until they confirm
Open the document without signing, read it fully, and sign only if nothing in it looks wrong
Sign it only after checking that the company logo on the document matches the real Narmada Steel logo
B.explanation: Attackers can send real DocuSign envelopes from their own accounts, so the real service does not prove the sender is real. Confirm with Narmada Steel through a number you already hold. A logo is easy to copy, and reading the document cannot tell you whether the request is genuine.

B.title: Question 6: Look-Alike Domains
B.scenario: What is a look-alike (spoofed) domain, for example rnicrosoft.com pretending to be microsoft.com?
options: An address made to look almost the same as a real company's address, by adding, swapping or changing a few characters, so people mistake it for the real one
A backup web address that a company registers so staff can still reach its site if the main one is down
An address that hides a person's identity by routing their emails through several servers
A temporary web address that IT creates to test new company applications before they go live
B.explanation: A look-alike domain copies a real name with small changes: an extra letter, a swapped letter, a missing letter, letters that merge (such as rn looking like m) or a different ending such as .co. Always read the whole domain, letter by letter.

B.title: Question 7: Suspicious Excel Attachment
B.scenario: A colleague you know well replies on a thread you started yesterday and attaches Vendor_Rates_Q4.xlsm with Enable Content to see the pricing. The email passes every check, but your colleague never uses macros. What is the best next step?

email.label: Message under review
email.subject: Re: Vendor rates for Q4
email.body:
Hi,
Please see the updated vendor rates attached. Open the file and select Enable Content to view the pricing correctly.
Thanks

options: Open the file in Protected View first, and enable content only if the macros look standard
Do not open it; confirm with your colleague by phone or Teams, and report it to IT security as a possible compromised account
Reply on the same thread asking whether the macros are needed, and wait for the answer before opening
Open the file on a test machine that has no company access, and enable content there
B.explanation: The reply may come from a real but compromised account, which is why it passes every check. Contact your colleague outside email and report it. Macros cannot be judged by how they look, and a test machine skips reporting.

B.title: Question 10: Two Genuine Company Updates
B.scenario: You receive two different emails from company departments. One is an HR benefits update and the other is a Facilities maintenance notice. Both use the company's genuine email domain and link to the appropriate internal company pages. Which email is legitimate?

emails.label: Email 1
emails.subject: Reminder: Update your employee benefits
emails.body:
Hello,
This is a reminder to review your employee benefits details for the upcoming year. Please use the employee portal to check your current selections.

emails.label: Email 2
emails.subject: Planned maintenance in the office
emails.body:
Hello,

options: Email 1 only
Email 2 only
Both emails are legitimate
Neither email is legitimate
B.explanation: Both emails use the correct fujisilvertech.com company domain, come from relevant company departments and link to company pages. The messages are different, but that does not make either one suspicious. Always check the sender and destination rather than assuming only one message can be genuine.

C.title: Question 1: AI Chatbot Impersonation
C.scenario: While searching for a software tool for work, a website opens a chat window where an AI assistant answers instantly and politely, then asks you to sign in with your work account to verify your licence. What is the key risk?

email.label: Website chat message
email.subject: Verify your work licence
email.body: Hello! I can help you verify your software licence. Please sign in with your company account to continue.

options: The chat is safe as long as it asks you to sign in rather than to download a file
A polite, instant chat does not prove the site is genuine, since AI can run convincing chats on fake sites, so sign in only on the official address you reached yourself
A convincing, fast chat means the website is genuine, since fake sites cannot run live chats
The chat is safe as long as the website address begins with https
C.explanation: AI chatbots can now run natural, helpful conversations on fake sites, so a good chat proves nothing. Reach the vendor through your own bookmark or the company portal. HTTPS only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest.

C.title: Question 2: Whaling
C.scenario: What is whaling, such as a fake email aimed at your company's Managing Director or CFO?
options: A phishing attack that is carried out through voice calls
A phishing attack that sends the same message to many employees at the same time
A phishing attack aimed at senior leaders such as the CEO or CFO, because they can approve large payments or access sensitive data
A phishing attack that uses fake wireless networks in public places
C.explanation: Whaling targets the big fish in a company. The mass-message option describes general phishing, the voice-call option is vishing, and the fake wireless network option describes a different attack.

C.title: Question 3: QR Phishing (Quishing)
C.scenario: A poster in the canteen shows a QR code for free staff benefits. What is QR phishing (also called quishing)?
options: Sending a harmful email attachment that contains a QR code inside it
Using a fake QR (Quick Response) code scanner app that steals your contacts
Hacking a company's QR code generator to change the prices it displays
Placing a malicious QR code in an email, poster or sticker so that scanning it takes you to a fake website or harmful download
C.explanation: In quishing the web address is hidden inside the QR image, so you cannot read it before scanning, and many email filters cannot read it either. Treat QR codes like links: only scan codes you trust.

emails.label: Email 2

emails.body:

Email 2 only
Both emails are legitimate
Neither email is legitimate
C.explanation: In Email 2 the link uses micr0soft.com with a zero instead of the letter o, and the text misspells Quarterly. Email 1 links to the genuine microsoft.com address.

C.title: Question 5: MFA Fatigue Attack
C.scenario: Late at night you receive six Multi-Factor Authentication approval prompts for your work account, then a call: This is the security team. We see repeated sign-in attempts on your account. Approve the next prompt to confirm it is you and we will lock the attacker out. What is the best action?

email.label: Related security message
email.subject: Urgent account security verification
email.body: This is the security team. We see repeated sign-in attempts on your account. Approve the next prompt to confirm it is you and we will lock the attacker out.

options: Deny all prompts and ask the caller for their employee ID before deciding whether to approve
Approve the next prompt once, because the caller already knows about the attempts and will block the attacker
Deny all prompts, hang up, report it to IT security using the official number, and change your password
Deny all prompts, wait for them to stop, and change your password in the morning
C.explanation: The caller is part of the attack: approving a prompt gives the attacker your sign-in. Deny, hang up, and report through an official number, then change your password. An employee ID is easy to fake, and waiting until morning leaves the attacker with a working password.

C.title: Question 6: Deepfake Finance Director
C.scenario: In a video call, your company's finance director asks you to release an urgent payment to a new vendor and to keep it quiet until a deal is announced. The face and voice match, the calendar invite came from their real account, and they answered your question about last week's meeting correctly. What is the best action?

email.label: Related payment request
email.subject: Urgent: New vendor payment
email.body: Please arrange the urgent payment to the new vendor today. Keep this confidential until the deal is announced. I will explain the details later.

options: Ask them to repeat the request in writing over the company chat system, then release the payment
Release the payment, because the invite, the voice and the answer to your question all check out
Pause the payment and confirm through the payment approval process and a directory phone number, since every check so far can be faked or compromised
Release half the payment now and the rest after confirming by email, to limit the risk
C.explanation: Faces, voices, invites and correct answers can all be faked or come from a compromised account, and secrecy with a new vendor is the real red flag. Use the approval process and a number from the directory. The same chat channel may be compromised, and paying half still loses money.

C.title: Question 7: Identify the Legitimate Expense Report Email
C.scenario: Both emails below appear to be sent from company expense addresses. Read the sender addresses and links carefully. Which email is legitimate?

emails.label: Email 1
emails.subject: Expense report #3391 needs your approval
emails.body:

An expense report submitted by a member of your team is waiting for your aproval.
Expenses Team

emails.label: Email 2
emails.subject: Expense report #3391 needs your approval
emails.body:
Hello,
An expense report submitted by a member of your team is waiting for your approval.

options: Email 1 only
Email 2 only
Both emails are legitimate
Neither email is legitimate
C.explanation: The real website name is the part just before the first single slash. In Email 1 that part ends in com-review.net, so fujisilvertech.com is only a decoy at the front. Email 1 also uses the different sender name expense instead of expenses and misspells approval. In Email 2 the link genuinely ends at fujisilvertech.com.

C.title: Question 8: Suspicious App Permissions
C.scenario: When you sign in to your work Microsoft 365 account, an app called Pipeline Insights asks to read and write all files, read mail and maintain access. The consent screen is on the real Microsoft sign-in page, shows a verified publisher badge, asks for no password, and the app was recommended in an email from a partner. What is the best action?

email.label: App permission request
email.subject: Recommended app for your project
email.body:
Hello,
We recommend Pipeline Insights to help with your project workflow. Please sign in and approve the requested permissions to activate the integration.

options: Accept only the read permissions and decline the write permission, since this limits what the app can change
Accept, then review the app's permissions after a week and remove it if it is not useful
Accept, because the consent screen is on the real Microsoft page and the publisher is verified
Decline, and ask IT security to review the app before anyone approves it, since the permissions are broad and the recommendation came by email
C.explanation: Consent phishing can use real Microsoft screens, and a verified badge does not make broad access safe. Access to files and mail should be reviewed by IT security first. Partial approval or a later review still gives the app access in the meantime.

C.title: Question 10: Supplier Bank Detail Fraud
C.scenario: A supplier emails new bank details to your accounts team's mailbox, from the same address as always. You call the phone number printed on the invoice and someone confirms the change. The new account is at a different bank, and the invoice is the one that carried the new number. What is the best action?

email.label: Message under review
email.subject: Updated bank details for upcoming payment
email.body:
Hello,
Please update our bank details for all future payments. Our account has changed due to an internal banking update. The new details are included in the attached invoice.
Regards,
Supplier Accounts Team

options: Update the details after your manager approves them by email
Hold the change and verify using a phone number from your supplier records or an earlier contract, not from the invoice or the email
Update the details, since a phone call confirmed the change
Update the details but send a small test payment first and check that it arrives
C.explanation: The number on the invoice came from the same email the attacker may control, so the call proves nothing. Verify with a number from your own records or an earlier contract. A manager's email approval and a test payment do not check who is behind the request.
